So, Witness, since you are feeling super, you are going to answer questions superbly, I hope, of the Prosecution and the Defence, but first it will be questions put by Mr. Keegan. Mr. Keegan, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, for the record, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Azedin Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your age, please?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I'm 38, going on to 39.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, what your profession was before 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I worked as a teacher of history and geography for eight years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what schools in the Prijedor area did you teach?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In Dusan Pantelic; Busnovi; and Bratstvo-Jedinstvo in Trnopolje, Brotherhood and Unity School.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the village of Busnovi, what was the majority of the population there, the majority of your students, what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Ninety-nine per cent were Serbs and Serb pupils. One per cent were Croat population or Croat pupils.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Brotherhood and Unity School in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The majority population was Muslim. Then came the Serbs, and there were some Russians, Bela-Russians, Ukrainians, some Croats, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you begin your teaching career? What year?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In 1984 in Busnovi, and in 1988 in Trnopolje, and for the last four years I worked simultaneously in Busnovi and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period between 1984 and 1992, did you have difficulty in either your classroom or with your colleagues based on ethnic problems or divisions between the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: 1979 to 1980 in Croatia, in the towns of Rijeka and Sisak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your compulsory duty were you a member of the reserve forces or the Territorial Defence in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did you do reserve duty? How often were you called up?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Once a year or once in two years. Sometimes twice in one year, sometimes once in two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of those call-ups? Were they local exercises?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Local exercises. Sometimes we would go outside the municipality of Prijedor, towards Podgradice but that was rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time that you were called up for reserve duty?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I think it was two or three years prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the elections in 1990, did you notice a difference in the nature of the relationship between you and your colleagues at work?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the nature of the change?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In 1991, when the war started in Croatia, most of my colleagues from work, and friends that I knew, were already wearing uniforms of the reserve forces of the then Yugoslav People's Army, and they had been on the battlefront in Slavonia, in Pakrac, and Lipik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this affect your relationship in the school with the staff?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: We still had relatively good relationships. However, the Serb members of the staff were becoming more and more secluded, and they talked amongst themselves only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a change in the reports in the media, on the television and the newspaper that also affected the relationship that you had with your colleagues at work?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb population was buying Serb press increasingly, coming from Belgrade, whereas we continued to buy the newspapers from Sarajevo, Oslobodjenje, Vecernje Novine, and so on. The Serbian press, coming from Belgrade, Ekspres Politika, Borba, Vecernje Novosti that is what they read. They also watched the Belgrade news programmes, and when the transmitters were destroyed, then we were cut off from other sources of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, could I just ask you to slow down a bit, please, in giving your answers to let the translators get all of your answer.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. You did not ask him his ethnicity, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I didn't, not yet, but I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, could you please answer the issue raised by Judge Riad? What is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak, a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your religious background?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to have discussions with was colleagues at work about this propaganda that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did. My colleagues at work were already wearing or were coming to work wearing the uniforms of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ask them why they were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask them, but I knew why they were wearing uniforms, because from what they said, it was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that made it clear to you why they were wearing those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That they would never allow Slovenia and Croatia or any other republic to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the 30th of April, 1992. You recall what occurred on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, I was at home or, rather, the night between the 29th and the 30th. And as usual, early the next morning, I was getting ready to go to work. That day I was due to work in the primary school in Trnopolje, the Brotherhood and Unity School. I worked two days a week in Busnovi, and three days a week in Trnopolje. The bus was due to leave around 6.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make your bus and get to work that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Because the Serb Crisis Staff and the Serb police and army, that night and that morning, took over power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out that the power had been taken over in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: On the road from my house to the town, to downtown, to the bus station, and railway station, there were many checkpoints manned by many policemen and soldiers, who were saying and -- stopping the travellers and telling them that that day there would be no work and that we should go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you returned home, did you listen to the radio that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I first went to have a cup of coffee with my colleagues from work in a well-known confectioner's, Kod Rame, and then I went home. A sweet shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got home, did you listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the announcements that were being made on the radio?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The radio, the announcer was Senija Dzafic, and the radio said that she was a Muslim traitor, and they were speaking on behalf of the Serb Crisis Staff, that that day, on the 30th of April of 1992, the Serb Crisis Staff, the Serb army, and the police had taken over power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the announcements did they indicate why they had taken over?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That the Serb people would no longer tolerate injustice, that the economics in the town of Prijedor and the municipality were bad, the economic situation, and that this step of taking over power and authority was justified with that end in mind. Over the radio, at the same time, Serb nationalistic songs and hymns were sung, Boze Pravde, God and Justice, and Tamo Daleko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Witness, Mr. Michael Keegan, but Mr. Krstan Simic would like to say something. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. I should just like to indicate an error in the translation, that is to say, a misunderstanding between Mr. Oklopcic and the translator. On page 27, 25th line, Mrs. Senija Dzafic said she was a Muslim traitor, and it was stated that this was proclaimed over the radio. So this is a slight misunderstanding, but it is an essential difference, a vital difference. So along those lines, perhaps the witness can correct himself and say what he stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Keegan, could you help us out here, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue raised is when you were speaking about the radio announcements, you identified the announcer on the radio.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the announcer?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Senija Dzafic, and she read an announcement on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you refer to her as a Muslim traitor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So they didn't -- she was not referred to as a Muslim traitor on the radio itself?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No, she wasn't, but she was, in view of the fact that she worked for that organisation. So automatically, in my opinion, she was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, I apologise for interrupting again. But I see that this question is a typical question for your cross-examination. You can intervene in your cross-examination and ask the witness to clarify what he meant. If you are going to interrupt when the witness -- may I put it this way: When the witness says something that isn't convenient to you, this results in confusion. So please take advantage of your cross-examination. And this seems to be a typical instance. So please ask your question, and the witness can clarify. I apologise once again, Mr. Keegan, but you may continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the 30th of April, were you able to return to work?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: A week or two later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify that, please? It was a week or two before you could return to work or you worked for another week or two?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I worked for another week or two, I think. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you stop working?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Because the right to work was taken away from me, and I was told that I was not conducive to the post and need no longer come to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was informed -- we were informed on the last day of the school, and it was in Trnopolje, in the school in Trnopolje. I don't remember exactly, but this was also broadcast over the radio. It was stated that all of us who were of a different religion and ethnic group need no longer come to work, and that only the vital organisations and enterprises of vital importance, which are vital, essential for the work of the municipality, for the functioning of the municipality could continue to function, like Elektroprijedor, the Zitopromet enterprise, and the enterprises of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the schools recessed early that year, earlier than scheduled?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On whose authority were they recessed early?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian part of the republic, which represented the interests of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the 22nd of May of 1992. Do you recall an incident that occurred on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That same afternoon, around the 22nd of May, we played a match and we called ourselves, our team, the Veterans against Predo, against the first team of Bereka, at the Bereka stadium. There were many of us there of different ethnicities, both Muslims and Serbs alike. Suddenly, after the first halftime, or thereabouts, from the Hambarine region, shooting was heard and smoke could be seen. As the crow flies, it is about two kilometres away, across, on the other bank of the Sana River, and the Bereka stadium was on the bank of the Sana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you later informed about what happened in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you given that information? How were you informed?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: From the stories people told and from television. The next day, Serb television announced publicly an interview with one of the wounded soldiers of the former Yugoslav army, who was lying in hospital in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same day that you saw that interview, then, the 23rd of May, was there a further attack?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Later on an ultimatum was posed to the population of Hambarine and the left bank of the Sana River that they had to give up policeman Aziz Aliskovic and two or three of his friends, who were at that checkpoint by Hambarine when this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened once the time for the ultimatum expired?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: It was 2.00 p.m. in the afternoon, by the clock, and shelling began of Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Carakine, and other villages in the surrounding area, which were on the left bank of the Sana River, from all directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this shelling began, where were you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was next to Berek, on the makeshift bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the shells as they landed in Hambarine and the other parts of Brdo?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where the shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the shelling coming from?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Topica hill, the Urije airport, and Brezicani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the translation, it says "Opica Brdo."

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. It's Topica Brdo, with a "T."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How were you able to tell that the shells were being fired from those positions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I know that very well because I lived in the area of Raskovac and Skela. And when I went to work, to Busnovi, on my way to work, I would pass by Gomjenica Cela. Topica Brdo is in front of Cela or a part of Cela, in fact. And the shells that flew over our heads were flying straight over our heads, in a straight line, which means that they could have been shot from the airport or from the barracks. And the shells that fell from the Brezicani area, Brezicani is on the way from Prijedor to Bosanski Novi, on that road. It is the first village from Prijedor, towards Bosanski Novi. They came from that direction as well. And that is two to three kilometres away from Brezicani, from Skela, Pecani, and Raskovac. And that is the area in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Hambarine, had there been publication about the location of artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there had, and other things. When the Serbs took over power on the 30th of April, 1992, publicly they published pictures and reports in the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper as to where all this weaponry was located; in the area of the airport, of the barracks, Urije airport, the barracks. And this was made available to the general public, so whoever wanted to could go and see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kozarski Vjesnik, is that the local paper published in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the attack on Hambarine, was there a subsequent attack on another area of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The Kozarac area, yes. In the Kozarac area. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that attack occur?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours, I think on the 24th or 25th. A day or two after the attack on Hambarine. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know what the majority of the population was in the village of Hambarine and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: 99.9999 per cent, they were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The same thing there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that would be a convenient moment. 12.50 is the time of the break; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. We are going to have a half hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. We will continue the hearing. Mr. Keegan, the floor is yours for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, before the break you described the attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac. I'd like to ask you, between the date of 29 April 1992 and the 30th of May, prior to the 30th of May, 1992, were there any attacks on Serbian villages or areas in the Prijedor municipality that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention now to the 30th of May, 1992. Where were you on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could I please have Exhibit 3/76 brought to the witness, that's the Prijedor town map, and if we could place it on the ELMO. If we could perhaps move the map up and to the right a bit, and up, please, if possible. Maybe just fold it so it moves up a bit. Up. THE USHER: Up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Up the screen. Okay. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, what area of Prijedor -- what was your neighbourhood referred to as? What area did you live in?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: My whole life I lived in a single street, and the name of that street was Rade Koncar 13. That is the part between Skela, and we called it Pecani or the area which was bordering on Berek, a small river which was, in fact, a confluence of the Sana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to the area where your home was on the map there, please.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates]. The street is Rade Koncar 13, and it went out onto Zarko Zgonjanin Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What occurred during the early morning hours of 30 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: There was strong shooting that could be heard all over, and shelling, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, when you first heard the shooting and the explosions, did you know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure, but I assumed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your assumption?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That there was an attempt to liberate the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later hear or did you later listen to the radio that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: At first I did not, but my wife told me and my father said that I should turn the radio on, which I did, and I listened to the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the announcements that were being made on the radio?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That there had been a conflict between the Serb army, the Territorial Defence with the units of the Mujahedin, the Muslim army, something like that, which according to the Serb radio station said that that so-called Mujahedin army had attempted to take over the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you listened to the radio, did they indicate whether or not the attack had been repelled or was under control?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself take part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you listened to the radio, was the population given any instructions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those instructions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That all who are loyal to the Serb authorities must hang out white flags on the roofs of their buildings and houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the radio indicate on whose authority those instructions were given?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did it indicate was issuing those instructions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: By the Serb staff, the Serb council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family comply with those instructions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did soldiers come to your neighbourhood that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Between 1.00 and 2.00 in the afternoon, after noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the soldiers doing when they came to your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They entered yards and ordered us to go out into the street and to head towards the old hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, your house had a white flag hanging on it?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went outside, did you notice whether other houses on your street had white flags on the houses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of your street?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The majority were Muslim. There were two Serb families and one mixed Serb-Croat. It's not important who was what, but, anyway, it was a mixed Serb-Croat family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other houses that had white flags on them, what ethnic group were the people who lived in those houses on your street?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Serbs. Could you please repeat that question once again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other houses on your street that had white flags hanging on them, what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serb houses that were on your street, did they have white flags on them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any difference in the way that the soldiers were treating the inhabitants of the houses that had white flags on them compared to those that did not have the white flags?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone forced to come out of the houses that did not have the white flags on your street?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who lived in those houses, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: You mean the houses where flags had not been hung up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers told you to go to the old hotel. Can you tell us what the name of that hotel was, please?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Balkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who came to your yard, did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of uniforms were those soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Mixed, camouflage green and blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where those forces were from, those that came to your street that day, that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The first group of soldiers who were in my street and on the road leading to the Balkan Hotel, or to be more precise, in Zarko Zgonjanin Street, were unknown to me. Later, just before we reached the Hotel Balkan, I recognised a couple of soldiers and policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything about the soldiers whom you did not recognise that gave you an indication of where they might be from?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The way they spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it about the way they spoke?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They used the Ekavica variant of the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the significance of the Ekavica dialect?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Until the war, Ekavica was never used in Bosnia. Only at certain courses of the so-called current Serbo-Croatian language was it taught or was the difference taught between the Ekavica and the Ijekavica dialects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What area of the former Yugoslavia did they normally speak the Ekavica dialect?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Serbia, Vojvodina, Montenegro, Sandzak, Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Ijekavica dialect, where was that traditionally spoken?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were being directed towards the Hotel Balkan, did you also see soldiers who you would later see in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that group of soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They were elite troops from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it that you saw them in Prijedor on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Between the three skyscrapers, the SDK bank, and the economic bank of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that that group of soldiers was from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was not aware of it, but during the first week of my stay in the Omarska concentration camp, they provided security for a part of the camp, which means those same special forces from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way to the hotel, did you see any buildings that were burning?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what areas did you see those buildings that were burning?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: In the area of the right-hand bank of the stream of Berek or the River Berek, and the area of the left bank of the Berek, the so-called Stari Grad or Old City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to that on the map, please, to that area?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: This is the left bank area, this is Stari Grad, and the left bank [indicated]. Stari Grad was an island, in fact, which had two small bridges on the river, linking Stari Grad with Skela on the one hand and the downtown centre on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, were you aware of the majority of the ethnic group that lived in the Stari Grad area?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the majority ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims and only one Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the area on the left bank of the Berek, as you refer to it, what was the majority ethnic group that lived in that region?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: All of them were Muslim. Along the Berek itself. That's what I'm talking about. Only along the Berek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the buildings that you saw burning, were you personally aware of the people who lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic group of the people who lived in or owned the buildings which you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies lying along the road as you were being directed to the Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you either know or did you later -- were you later told the identity of those people?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, but I had my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what your assumptions were for us of who those bodies were?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I can. On the road, as I came out of my street, as I just said, the name of the street was Rade Koncar. We first reached the main road, which was called Zarko Zgonjanin Street. A part of that street or, rather, the left part of that Zarko Zgonjanin Street included a part of the market. On the pavement itself, I was walking together with my son, and out of fear I didn't notice anything; however, my son asked me later on, "Daddy, what is this on the ground next to the pavement?" I looked, and those were two charred bodies. I took him by the hand, turned his face away, and continued walking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able -- later, were you told or informed about who the victims were at that spot?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That same moment, a wooden kiosk was on fire. It was roughly ten metres away from the bodies. Obviously, it had been hit with a Zolja or something like that, a hand-held rocket launcher, and I assumed that those were two Albanians who used to sell snacks and coffee there. But I wasn't sure, and at the time that did not really interest me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other bodies on your way whose identity was confirmed to you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: On my way, we were stopped at a plateau surrounded by three skyscrapers in the very centre of the town, the economic bank and the SDK bank. At that moment I didn't see any other bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were being directed to the Hotel Balkan, did you walk past buildings where your Serb neighbours lived?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, were those Serb neighbours doing as you went by?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They were spitting at us. And if I may be rude, they swore our Muslim and Alija's mothers and poured water on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your group arrived at the Hotel Balkan, approximately how many other people did you see there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those people, did you see some that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parts of Prijedor did those people come from that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Stari Grad, Skela, Raskovac, Pecani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of those people whom you could recognise?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Virtually all were Muslims, and a couple of Croats here and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: First of all, all his life he was a regular police officer, that was one reason; and the other, he was married to a Muslim who was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of Miroslav Kvocka's family at the Hotel Balkan -- any of his wife's family? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I saw three brothers of his wife, his wife's three brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the people, you and the others who were brought there with you, were gathered at the Hotel Balkan, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They separated the men from the women and the children and they started boarding them onto buses, which had been parked in front of the old Hotel Balkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "They separated the men from the women ... and they started boarding them onto the buses." Who is "they" who was boarding them onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The police, the Serb police, and the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was being put onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Adult males, ranging between 18, or maybe 16, to 60 years of age. But there were some children too who were very tall for their age, so that even though they were younger, they were included in the group. Old men of 65 and 70 years of age were not taken, as far as I know; they were left behind in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the buses go when they left the Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: My bus, or the bus I was in, started and then stopped in front of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the SUP? What is that building?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: It is the building of the police. Before the war, it was called the Internal Affairs Service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The bus stopped; the door opened. A couple of drunken soldiers got in, who had been standing in front of the SUP building and on the plateau in front of the municipality building, and they started beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there already an escort or guard on the bus when those other soldiers got in?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No. But later on two escorts climbed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who got in and started beating, who were they beating?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Anyone they happened to lay their hands on, whoever came first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they hitting the Muslim men who had been put on the bus at the hotel with you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they hitting these men with?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: With batons and rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating continue for?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Maybe 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it stop?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Because these two guards or escorts climbed in, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the bus -- excuse me. Were you beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the buses go from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: At that moment when we started off, I wasn't aware where we were going, but later I saw that we were passing through Gomjenica, Cela, Rakelici, Busnovi. And we reached the crossroads, but virtually at the end of the road, the road leads straight ahead to the Tomasica mine, and the other end leads to Busnovi, Krivaja, Maricka, and from then on to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to publish now a Chamber exhibit, Exhibit 1/26. It is a map of the Prijedor area. If we could bring it down just a bit, please. There we go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, on this map, please, could you point out the route that you just described, from Prijedor, through Gomjenica, Cela, et cetera, the way you were taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Prijedor [indicates], Gomjenica [indicates], Cela [indicates], Rakelici [indicates], Tomasica [indicates]. As you can see here, this is almost the end of the road, and this is the entrance to the Tomasica mine. The other part of the road continues on towards Omarska, a part towards Krivaja, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the villages that are along that road, are you aware of the majority of the ethnic group that lived in those villages that you've named?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the villages the village where you taught school?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Practically -- yes, that was Busnovi. And almost all the children who came to the central school of Busnovi would come from the middle, upper, and lower Maricka, from Krivaja and Tomasica. We had three district schools in addition to the central school, and they are the schools of Gornja, Sredna, and Donja Maricka, upper, middle, and lower Maricka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you also point out on that map where Hambarine is?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I can, yes. Hambarine is on the left-hand side of the Sana River. That is Rizvanovici [indicates], Rakovscani [indicates], Biscani [indicates], Hambarine [indicates], and this road leading down towards Donja Ljubija [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kozarac, you also referred to Kozarac earlier. Could you indicate where that is, please.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I can. This is the road Kozarusa [indicates], Kozarac, and further on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The road that you were just pointing to, what was that road referred to? How was that road referred to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: You mean when I came to Busnovi and Tomasica, that road?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The road that goes past Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That is the Prijedor-Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were riding in the bus to Omarska, were you able to look out the window of the bus?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the condition of those villages, the villages you described as having a majority of Serbs in their population. Can you describe what condition those villages were in.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That road between Busnovi and Omarska, it is a macadamised road surface, not asphalt, and it connected Tomasica and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any signs of damage or burning houses or any other indication that there had been any conflict or battle in those areas?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did the buses stop on that day? What was your final destination?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the model in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They are the former premises of the Omarska concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have the witness approach the model, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, could you please indicate on the model the area of the camp where the buses that you were on came into the camp on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Most of the buses stopped in front of the central building [indicated]. That's what it was known as. But there was always one which was separated from the others, which means that the bus from which at that moment the so-called passengers got out -- let us call them passengers, because at the time they were passengers. I don't know what else to call them -- when they got out, stepped down onto the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a bus unloading in front of your bus when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see that bus, watch it unloading?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the instructions given to that bus? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those instructions?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That the so-called passengers or people on the bus, that is to say, in this bus here facing the pista [indicated], could get out onto the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As those prisoners were brought onto the pista, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: When this bus had unloaded, so to speak, the people from this bus, then it was my bus' turn, and it too had parked in practically the same spot. Later on, we were ordered to go out onto the pista ourselves. At that particular moment, when we started getting out of this bus here, there was some terrible shooting. We were ordered to get back into the buses immediately and to lower our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to actually see the shooting?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, was your bus finally ordered to unload into the pista?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, after some time had passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you were unloaded onto the pista, did you see any indications or results of that shooting?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: There was blood on the asphalt, and soldiers and policemen who, with hoses, were washing the area, the middle part of the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the shooting, do you recall if there were any other vehicles in the area of the pista, other than your bus?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once your group was onto the pista, what instructions were you given?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That five of us should go to this side and turn our faces towards the wall, and another five on this side, and that they too should turn to face this wall here, turn towards the wall here [indicated].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened to the prisoners who were up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to leave all our gold jewellery, our watches, and all the money we had with us at that time, the money that was on us and all the other things, and to hand everything over to the policemen who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners being beaten during this time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Some of them. There would be a kick in the back, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you had given all your valuables and been searched on the wall, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: We had to go to the largest building, the central building, the canteen or restaurant, which was located here [indicated].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened once you got inside the building?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: It was said, that is, there were already a large number of detainees, that is to say, people. We didn't know we would be prisoners yet, at least as far as I was concerned, I don't know about the others, but there were many of them here, and they were talking about the shooting that had happened on the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know any of the people who had been on that bus in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any relatives of yours on that bus?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was on that bus?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: You mean of my relatives?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: My relative from Klopcic, Muharem Hare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: That a father and son had been killed. Kapetanovic Avdo and Asaf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to going into that room, did you have to give your personal information to anyone?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Not at that moment, just my ID, money, watch, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of the accused persons in this case were present in the camp when you arrived there on the pista?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: You mean the ones here who are in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Miro Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Miroslav Kvocka doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: He had separated Rizo Crnalic, nicknamed Rizak, brother-in-law. He had singled him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can return to your seat now. The room that you were placed in that evening, that first night, did the prisoners later give that room a name? Was it known by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Later on, it got name of Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Mujo's room that evening?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They took me to the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay on the pista that night?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The entire night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of the prisoners remain on the pista that night?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the other prisoners who didn't stay out there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Some of them were returned to Mujo's room, and some, or the majority, were sent to the main or largest building of the concentration camp at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the building referred to as the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any food or water that evening?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive your first meal?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: A day later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first get the opportunity to get some water, some refreshment?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Also the day after. But we personally had to ask permission to go and get water and to use the water ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the meal that you received, your first meal?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Well, the water from the boiled potatoes and perhaps a leaf of cabbage in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any bread?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: A piece of bread which was not fresh. It was stale bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given anything to drink with your meal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but I see Mr. Simic on his feet. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] An objection, Your Honour. There is an objection to the transcript a moment ago, and the contents of what was contained. Just the "water" was entered into the transcript. There were "two potatoes," I believe. So could the witness be asked to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Keegan, could you ask the question again so that we have the entire LiveNote corrected? Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, could you again please describe what was the first meal you received? What was in it?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: The first meal which I received, I don't remember exactly, but all the other meals consisted of a couple of leaves of salad in water, two or three small potatoes in water, and sometimes beans or -- beans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My following question to that was: Did you receive anything to drink with your meal?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the nature or the quality of the meals ever improve during your stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in the camp, did you have access to -- excuse me. Did the guards eat the same food as the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of food did the guards receive?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They received pieces of meat, paste for their in-between meal, salami, beer, and cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they receive vegetables with their food?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they drink water from the same water taps or same sources as the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have access to water and to toilets?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, if we were to raise two fingers or our hand and ask permission to, ask the guards on shift, on duty, on the pista. Otherwise, those of us who were on the pista could not go without asking permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was permission always given when you asked?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the guards organised in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: There were three shifts and each shift had a certain number of guards. Above that shift or shifts, there was a deputy -- no, I apologise, there was the shift leader. And above them, that is, the guard and the shift leader, there would be the deputy commander of the camp, or the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the camp, did you learn the names of the three shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the names of the three shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Gruban, nicknamed Ckalja; Krkan, nicknamed Radic [as interpreted]; Milojica Kos, nicknamed Krle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript indicates that Krkan's nickname was Radic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No. That's his surname. "Krkan" was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the surname was, of that person?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Radic. Radic. His name was Mladen, his first name, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these three guard shifts, did the different shifts act differently in allowing prisoners access to water and toilets?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Practically all in the same way. However, the worst, if there can be something worse than the worst, was Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way was Krkan's shift the worst?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: They beat people most and mistreated them most and killed them most, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any effect on this shift's actions in people going to the toilet or asking for water?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that effect?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Many of them didn't dare go to the toilet, so they relieved themselves in their pants, both passing a stool and urinating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wouldn't many of the prisoners dare to go to the toilets on Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Because they would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the camp, were you allowed to bathe or to shave or to wash your clothes?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the water taps in the camp that you had access to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: One tap was in front of Mujo's bedroom, or central building, and from there, 100 or 200 metres was a hose of some kind where water came out of. The taps were also next to the canteen, in the central building, where there were two or three toilets. And there were also toilets in the hangar building, where there were four or five toilets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The water that you had access to, that you described on the outside, the one outside of the administration building and the one you said was further away, about 100 metres away, was that water drinkable water? Was it fresh water?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: We drank it; the guards didn't drink it. What the water was like, I can't really say, and why we drank it whereas they did not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did disease and sickness become a problem in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of sickness or diseases did the prisoners get?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Dysentery, rashes and itching, mange. Psychological and physical injuries on the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did lice become a problem?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the prisoners deal with these problems, the dysentery and the other problems you described, the other illnesses?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC
utterances.text: A small number of prisoners had a few tablets of some kind; I don't know exactly what they were. But us others just waited for it to go away of its own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Keegan. It is, indeed, time to break. We are going to interrupt the sitting for today, and we will continue the hearing tomorrow at 9.30, as provided for. Witness, we meet again tomorrow. Goodbye until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25
